transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Lydia (Cedar Bank CTO), Ben (Head of Ops), Anita (Dir Security)

Summary (auto): quick review of BCDR, SLA targets and escalation process, agreed follow-ups to send docs and run a tabletop failover test

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm maya, i'm the account lead for cedar bank. we also have carlos from our infra team.
[00:08] Lydia: thanks maya, appreciate it. we'll keep this focused — the security team wants clarity on rto/rpo, how you handle failover, and what the escalation ladder looks like.
[00:20] Carlos: yep, happy to walk through. quick note — i'll call out that some product names in my notes might auto-correct, so if you see things like K-V cache or kv-cache spelled weird that's the same.
[00:29] Ben: cool, main ask from ops is minimizing customer-impacting downtime. we need to know realistic rto/rpo numbers for our inference endpoints and the process if a region goes down.
[00:40] Carlos: for hosted mode we target a service-level uptime of 99.95% for production endpoints by default; for dedicated we can contract 99.99% with reserved capacity and cross-region failover options. rto for a full region outage depends on whether you want automatic failover vs manual switch — automatic is typically in the 2 to 10 minute ballpark for our traffic routing; manual failover with verification is closer to 15–60 minutes.
[01:10] Anita: wait, 2 to 10 minutes for automatic — what's required on our side? do we need to run any proxies or change dns ttl?
[01:18] Carlos: good question. for automatic cross-region failover we use active routing with health checks; dns ttl changes are minimal because we route at the network/admission layer, but you will need a peered networking setup if you're on private deployment (VPC). we'll share the network diagrams.
[01:33] Lydia: what's the rpo on that? for some of our fraud models we can't afford losing more than a minute of state.
[01:38] Carlos: RPO is near zero for live KV cache backed models because we replicate model state across replicas; for model artifacts we keep continuous syncs and snapshots — RPO for persistent state is under 5 minutes in cross-region mode, and we can tighten that in dedicated contracts with synchronous replication.
[01:56] Ben: and backups? retention and restore time?
[02:00] Carlos: backups are incremental. config and model snapshots are retained per your retention policy — by default 30 days, can be extended. restore time for a typical model snapshot and config is usually 30–90 minutes depending on size; however, for the hot path we rely on replication to reduce restore needs.
[02:18] Anita: ok, switching to incident process: who is paged at Redwood? severity definitions?
[02:23] Maya: we follow a sev1/sev2/sev3 taxonomy. sev1 is full production outage affecting all customers, immediate phone + p1 page, we engage engineering leads and exec on-call. sev2 is degraded performance or partial outage, page to on-call, depending on impact we escalate to se and ae. sev3 is informational.
[02:41] Carlos: we integrate with PagerDuty and can ingest your escalation policies. our on-call rotations are published, and we provide a 24/7 escalation path for sev1 through our enterprise SLA.
[02:52] Lydia: can we map the severity to our business impact matrix? we need to ensure our internal compliance can connect severity to compensating controls.
[02:58] Maya: yes we can include a mapping doc. we'll draft a table mapping cedar bank impact tiers to our severities and proposed communication cadence.
[03:08] Ben: audit logs — we need immutable logs for all admin actions and model deployments, and a way to stream to our SIEM.
[03:15] Carlos: audit logs are available for all control plane actions, with timestamps, actor, and ip. we support log forwarding via syslog or direct cloud logging export. retention configurable; immutable snapshots possible on dedicated/private deployments.
[03:29] Anita: encryption and KMS — do you use customer-managed keys? key rotation? hsm?
[03:34] Carlos: yes, we support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations for hosted and definitely for private. we support bring-your-own-key and can integrate with HSM providers for FIPS and stricter requirements. key rotation policies are configurable; we store encrypted at rest and in transit with TLS 1.2/1.3.
[03:50] Lydia: data residency — our data must stay inside country A for certain models. is that supported?
[03:55] Maya: we have region pinning and private deployment options. for strict residency we recommend our private control plane in your VPC or an on-prem package. we'll include the residency matrix in the docs.
[04:06] Ben: SLA credits — what's the credit model and time to payout?
[04:10] Maya: standard SLA credit model is monthly credit proportional to downtime bucket. payout is processed within 30 days after customer claim and verification; for enterprise contracts we can negotiate different remedies.
[04:23] Anita: escalation contact list — can you walk through how incident comms look? who owns customer comms?
[04:29] Maya: in a sev1 we spin up a war room, engineering lead provides technical updates, AE owns customer comms and exec updates, and CS/solutions eng supports runbooks. we push status to your preferred channel (pager, email, status page).
[04:44] Carlos: technical escalation includes our infra on-call, then platform leads, then SRE managers, then if needed execs. we publish runbooks and postmortems; postmortems are available to enterprise customers with redacted internal info if requested.
[04:58] Lydia: speaking of postmortem, what does your timeline look like?
[05:02] Carlos: initial incident timeline within 24 hours, a full postmortem draft within 7 business days, and a final postmortem after internal review typically within 14 days.
[05:12] Ben: about testing — we want a tabletop and a full failover test. how do you run those?
[05:17] Carlos: tabletop is usually a 90-minute scenario walk-through with stakeholders; failover test can be a planned disruption in lower env, or a production failover window for an agreed time. we provide a test plan, rollback steps, and can coordinate a blackout window.
[05:32] Anita: do you do runbooks for us or do we author them?
[05:35] Maya: we'll provide vendor runbooks and a template; we can help tailor them to cedar bank and run a joint tabletop to validate.
[05:43] Lydia: compliance artifacts — SOC2, ISO, penetration test results — can you share?
[05:48] Maya: yes — we'll send the current SOC2 attestation, ISO summary, and the most recent pentest exec summary under NDA.
[05:56] Ben: we also need to confirm who has admin rights and RBAC controls for model deployments.
[06:01] Carlos: we support RBAC with role templates, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and audit trail for admin actions. for dedicated/private you can enforce stricter RBAC and limited admin scopes.
[06:14] Anita: one last question — during an incident, how do you handle cached KV state for low-latency models? is there a risk of split brain?
[06:21] Carlos: KV cache uses a leaderless replication with consistent hashing and tombstones to avoid split brain in most failure modes; in cross-region failover we promote replicas with a handoff protocol to ensure consistency. for absolute zero-loss you can enable synchronous replication at the cost of write latency; we can discuss tradeoffs in the follow-up.
[06:45] Maya: ok, quick recap and next steps. we'll send the BCDR runbook, draft SLA amendment, and the network diagrams for peering; carlos will share the failover test plan and propose windows, and anita will send the on-call matrix. schedule the tabletop week of 7/20.
[07:02] Lydia: good, expecting docs by 7/10.
[07:06] Maya: noted. thanks all, we'll follow up over email and upload artifacts to the shared folder.
[07:12] Ben: thanks everyone.
